title: Healthy Versus Pathology Comparison
subtitle: Compare variation, dysfunction, injury and disorder without treating a scan as a diagnosis
altText: Accessible chalkboard-style comparison of two overlapping brain network maps: one shows variable healthy organisation and the other shows structural, functional, developmental, vascular and degenerative patterns, joined by a clinical-context bridge.
learningObjectives: Distinguish healthy variation, dysfunction, injury and disorder using clinical context rather than a binary normal-abnormal label.
Compare structural, functional, developmental, vascular and degenerative patterns without assuming that imaging establishes diagnosis.
Interpret symptoms through distributed networks, pathways, time course and reserve.
Identify limitations and uncertainty when relating a biological finding to a person's presentation.

sections.explainSimply: Healthy brains vary. A difference on a scan may be harmless, while important dysfunction may occur without a visible structural lesion. Pathology becomes clinically meaningful through pattern, time course, symptoms and context.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Variation describes differences within expected diversity; dysfunction is impaired operation; injury is damage caused by an event; disorder is a clinically defined syndrome involving distress, impairment or risk. These categories overlap but are not interchangeable, and none can be inferred from imaging alone.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Comparison requires converging evidence from history, examination, cognitive or psychological assessment, laboratory data, structural and functional imaging, longitudinal change and differential diagnosis. Structural abnormalities may be incidental; functional changes may be state-dependent or nonspecific; developmental organisation may differ without representing acquired damage; vascular lesions follow time and territory; degenerative disease is supported by progressive clinical and biomarker patterns. Network disconnection, diaschisis, compensation, reserve and comorbidity shape phenotype.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A city map and a traffic report: street layout, current flow, construction damage and long-term decline describe different things, and none alone tells you how one resident is functioning.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Careful framing prevents biological essentialism, false reassurance from an unremarkable scan, and overdiagnosis from incidental findings. It supports formulation that integrates cognition, emotion, behaviour, daily function, development and medical context.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Acute infarction can disrupt a vascularly organised network; traumatic axonal injury can disconnect systems beyond a focal lesion; epilepsy, migraine or metabolic disturbance can alter function transiently; developmental differences shape network organisation; degeneration evolves across connected systems. Similar symptoms can arise through different mechanisms, and similar findings can have different consequences.
sections.clinicalPearl: Treat imaging as one source of evidence: ask whether the finding, time course, network and examination converge before attributing a symptom or diagnosis.
sections.practicalExample: Compare an incidental small arachnoid cyst in a well person, transient network dysfunction during migraine aura, focal tissue injury after an MCA infarct, a developmental language disorder and progressive medial temporal-network degeneration. The clinically useful distinction comes from convergence, not appearance alone.
sections.limitationsCautions: Normal ranges depend on age, development, acquisition method and reference population. Group-level biomarkers often overlap across individuals and diagnoses. Absence of a visible lesion does not exclude dysfunction, while an abnormal-looking finding may be incidental. Avoid value-laden language and deterministic normal-versus-abnormal conclusions.

anatomy.position: Whole-brain comparison across cortex, subcortex, white matter, vascular territories and large-scale functional networks.
anatomy.spatialRelationships: Local tissue findings sit within connected systems; remote effects may occur through white-matter disconnection, diaschisis, altered excitation-inhibition balance and compensatory recruitment.
outputs: need for monitoring or urgent action
anatomy.bloodSupply: Vascular change is interpreted by onset, arterial territory, collateral supply and tissue evolution. Chronic small-vessel disease and incidental vascular variants require clinical correlation.
anatomy.lesionEffects: Effects depend on lesion mechanism, location, volume, laterality, white-matter involvement, distributed network disruption, premorbid reserve and recovery; a lesion does not map one-to-one onto a symptom.
psychologicalPresentations: distress shaped by interpretation and context
no impairment despite an incidental finding
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: A healthy-pathology comparison can organise hypotheses and urgency, but diagnosis requires concordance among clinical phenotype, course, examination and appropriately interpreted tests.

explorerParts.label: Healthy variation & reserve
explorerParts.detail: Brain morphology, lateralisation, connectivity and performance vary with age, development, experience and measurement conditions.
explorerParts.clinical: Use appropriate norms and functional evidence before labelling a variant pathological.

explorerParts.label: Structural change
explorerParts.detail: Atrophy, mass effect, altered signal, malformation or white-matter change describes structure, not by itself cause, severity or diagnosis.
explorerParts.clinical: Correlate location and chronicity with symptoms; consider incidental findings, artefact and alternative causes.

explorerParts.label: Functional dysfunction
explorerParts.short: Operation can change without a fixed lesion
explorerParts.detail: Network physiology can vary with seizure activity, migraine, medication, sleep, pain, metabolic state and psychiatric state.
explorerParts.clinical: Functional measures are often state-dependent and group-derived; they should support rather than replace clinical assessment.

explorerParts.label: Developmental difference
explorerParts.detail: Developmental timing, plasticity and experience shape network organisation and skill acquisition across childhood and adulthood.
explorerParts.clinical: Establish developmental history and adaptive impact; avoid describing all atypical organisation as damage.

explorerParts.label: Vascular injury
explorerParts.detail: Ischaemia and haemorrhage disrupt tissue according to vessel anatomy, collateral flow, lesion evolution and connected pathways.
explorerParts.clinical: Sudden focal deficits require urgent stroke assessment; imaging pattern assists but does not replace bedside evaluation.

explorerParts.label: Degenerative network change
explorerParts.detail: Neurodegenerative processes often spread through vulnerable cell populations and connected networks rather than respecting one isolated region.
explorerParts.clinical: Diagnosis depends on progressive phenotype, exclusion of mimics and, when appropriate, validated biomarkers.

interactions.label: Select a structure or network comparison

quiz.question: Which statement best distinguishes an imaging finding from a diagnosis?
options: A finding becomes diagnostic only when appropriately combined with clinical and other evidence
Functional imaging independently establishes psychiatric diagnosis
quiz.rationale: Imaging is one evidence source; diagnosis depends on validated criteria and convergence with phenotype, course and examination.

quiz.question: Which description of dysfunction is most accurate?
options: Impaired operation may occur with or without a visible structural lesion
It always means irreversible tissue destruction
It is identical to a disorder
It can be inferred from one group-average biomarker
quiz.rationale: Physiological dysfunction may be transient, state-dependent or structurally occult and is not synonymous with injury or disorder.

quiz.question: Why can similar lesions produce different outcomes?
options: Network extent, laterality, reserve, development, comorbidity and recovery differ
Every symptom belongs to one brain region
quiz.rationale: Clinical effects emerge from distributed systems and individual context, not lesion location alone.

quiz.question: What most strongly supports a degenerative interpretation?
options: A progressive clinical phenotype with a concordant longitudinal pattern and appropriate exclusion of mimics
quiz.rationale: Degenerative diagnosis rests on progression and converging clinical evidence, sometimes supported by validated biomarkers.

spacedRepetition.reviewPrompt: Distinguish variation, dysfunction, injury and disorder, then explain why imaging alone cannot establish diagnosis.

accessibility.screenReaderSummary: Interactive whole-brain comparison of healthy variation with structural, functional, developmental, vascular and degenerative change, including clinical uncertainty and network effects.

lesionLab.title: Healthy variation or pathology?
lesionLab.instruction: Decide which explanatory frame best fits the pattern. The answer emphasises why a single scan or score is not enough.

cases.label: Incidental
cases.prompt: Imaging shows a stable anatomical variant, but the person has no concordant neurological signs, cognitive decline or functional change.
cases.rationale: A structural difference without a concordant clinical phenotype may represent healthy variation or an incidental finding rather than disease.
cases.caveat: Clinical significance depends on the specific finding, history and appropriate medical interpretation.

cases.label: Acute focal
cases.prompt: A previously well person develops sudden unilateral weakness and language difficulty over minutes.
cases.rationale: A sudden focal neurological syndrome is a vascular emergency pattern until proven otherwise, and time course is as important as location.
cases.caveat: Stroke mimics exist, but emergency assessment should not be delayed while attempting to resolve the differential.

cases.label: Progressive
cases.prompt: Cognitive and behavioural abilities decline progressively over years with increasing functional dependence and a coherent network-level pattern.
cases.rationale: A progressive, patterned decline raises a neurodegenerative hypothesis, which is evaluated longitudinally alongside reversible causes and, when indicated, biomarkers.
cases.caveat: Progressive symptoms do not identify a specific disease by themselves; psychiatric, medical, medication and sleep-related contributors require assessment.

clinicalComparison.title: Compare normal variation with disrupted systems
clinicalComparison.instruction: Switch between qualified examples. Keep normal variation, compensation and context separate from pathology.

comparisons.label: Functional network change

healthy.label: Flexible network recruitment
healthy.summary: Distributed systems change their coupling with task demands and state.
healthy.mechanism: Dynamic recruitment and inhibition support efficient switching between networks.
healthy.observable: Performance varies with task load while core function remains broadly adaptive.

pathology.label: Inefficient or disrupted recruitment
pathology.summary: A network may become less efficient, less selective or poorly coordinated with other systems.
pathology.mechanism: Altered connectivity, node dysfunction or state effects can disturb coordinated processing.
pathology.observable: Slowed, inconsistent or context-sensitive cognitive performance may emerge.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: The clinically useful question is not whether a network looks different, but whether the difference converges with history, examination and functional impairment.
comparisons.assessment: Compare performance across tasks and contexts, look for converging cognitive patterns, and consider fatigue, mood, medication and validity.
comparisons.caveat: Functional differences are not diagnostic biomarkers on their own and may reflect state, development, compensation or measurement noise.

comparisons.label: Vascular disruption

healthy.label: Intact perfusion
healthy.summary: Neural tissue receives sufficient blood flow to support local computation and connected network function.
healthy.mechanism: Arterial supply and autoregulation maintain oxygen and substrate delivery.
healthy.observable: No focal deficit attributable to acute regional hypoperfusion.

pathology.label: Focal vascular injury
pathology.summary: Ischaemia or haemorrhage can damage local tissue and interrupt fibres passing through the region.
pathology.mechanism: Tissue injury plus oedema, disconnection and remote network effects shape the phenotype.
pathology.observable: Abrupt focal neurological and cognitive changes may occur, depending on territory and extent.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: Time course and neurological pattern are central to vascular reasoning; the same cognitive symptom can arise from different territories or mechanisms.
comparisons.assessment: Pair neuropsychological findings with onset, neurological signs, imaging and vascular history rather than reverse-inferring a lesion from a test score.
comparisons.caveat: Vascular territories overlap and symptoms evolve with reperfusion, oedema, diaschisis and recovery.

comparisons.label: Degenerative change

healthy.label: Age-related change
healthy.summary: Some slowing and variability can occur with ageing without constituting neurodegenerative disease.
healthy.mechanism: Normal ageing involves heterogeneous biological and cognitive changes with substantial individual variation.
healthy.observable: Mild slowing may coexist with preserved everyday independence and stable learned knowledge.

pathology.label: Progressive neurodegenerative pattern
pathology.summary: Disease processes progressively compromise vulnerable neural systems and connected functions.
pathology.mechanism: Pathology accumulates over time and affects networks according to disease-specific and individual factors.
pathology.observable: Progressive decline, loss of previously established abilities and increasing functional impact may appear.

comparisons.clinicalMeaning: Trajectory and loss of function matter more than a single low score when distinguishing normal variation from progressive disease.
comparisons.assessment: Use collateral history, serial change, functional status, medical work-up and domain pattern alongside normative interpretation.
comparisons.caveat: Age, education, sensory factors, mood, sleep, medication and premorbid ability can mimic or magnify apparent decline.

assessmentLab.title: Assessment-linked healthy/pathology reasoning
assessmentLab.instruction: Use trajectory, functional impact and converging evidence to distinguish variation from clinically significant change.

cases.label: Functional change
cases.prompt: A person reports cognitive difficulty but structural imaging is unremarkable. What assessment domain best determines whether there is meaningful dysfunction?
cases.rationale: Normal structural imaging does not exclude dysfunction; significance comes from reproducible cognitive/behavioural change, time course and real-world impact.
supports: objective change converging with functional decline
time course compatible with the hypothesised mechanism
challenges: symptoms tracking primarily with sleep, stress or medication state
lack of functional impact despite subjective concern
cases.nextStep: Use longitudinal and multimethod evidence; investigate reversible contributors and do not treat a normal scan as proof of normal function.
cases.caveat: Objective tests can also be normal despite genuine intermittent or context-dependent impairment; absence of a test abnormality is not proof that symptoms are unreal.

cases.label: Vascular change
cases.prompt: A patient develops abrupt focal cognitive and neurological change. What should anchor the assessment?
cases.targetDomain: Time-locked focal neurological and cognitive profile
options: Time-locked focal neurological and cognitive profile
cases.rationale: Abrupt onset and focal signs make vascular localisation and urgent medical assessment higher priority than broad trait-level psychological interpretation.
observe: focal weakness, sensory or visual signs
vascular risk and acute medical context
taskTypes: brief focal cognitive screening when medically appropriate
later targeted neuropsychological assessment for recovery planning
challenges: non-focal fluctuating symptoms better explained by systemic state
cases.nextStep: Acute stroke-like presentations require emergency medical pathways; detailed neuropsychological assessment follows stabilisation.
cases.caveat: Small, strategic or posterior-circulation events can be clinically significant despite subtle early findings.

cases.label: Degenerative change
cases.prompt: A family reports gradual progressive decline over several years. Which assessment feature is most informative for distinguishing disease-related change from stable individual variation?
options: A single low score in isolation
cases.rationale: Neurodegenerative hypotheses depend on decline from prior functioning and a coherent evolving profile, not simply low performance relative to norms.
supports: evolving pattern compatible with a disease network
challenges: performance normalises when mood, sleep or medication factors improve
no corroborated functional change over time
cases.nextStep: Integrate serial cognitive data with medical work-up, informant history and functional trajectory.
cases.caveat: Normal ageing, psychiatric illness, sensory impairment, medication effects and medical disease can mimic or amplify cognitive decline.
